reader.title: Hodge house shooting
bases: A band of white men fired into a Black man's house at night and killed his mother; no accusation, custody or announced lynching purpose is reported (A1).
One four-sentence Louisville dispatch printed in one paper is the only report found in either press (A1).

summary.text: The Hodge house shooting was a night attack in August 1880 in which a band of white men fired on a Black man named Hodge in his house and killed his eighty-year-old mother.
It was reported in a Louisville, Kentucky, dispatch, which said the killers had not been found.
According to the dispatch, dated early on Friday, August 20, the attack took place "last Wednesday night," which was August 18.
Hodge, described as "a negro," was inside his house when "a band of white men" fired upon him.
His mother, whose name was not given, was shot and killed.
The dispatch did not say where the house stood, how many men were in the band, whether Hodge was wounded, or what reason, if any, the attackers had.
Hodge said he thought he could trace the men who had killed his mother, but at the time of the report "they have not yet been found."
No report of an inquest, an arrest or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The only account found is a four-sentence special dispatch from Louisville that the Omaha Daily Bee printed on its front page on August 20, among short wire items on a lightning fire in the Pennsylvania oil fields and a murder trial in San Francisco.
The Bee set the item under the headline "White Devils" and called the attackers "the murderers," language that placed blame on the white band rather than on the victims.
No coverage in the Black press and no Kentucky paper's report of the shooting was found.

accounts.label: Louisville special dispatch
accounts.gist: A band of white men fired on Hodge in his house on Wednesday night, killing his eighty-year-old mother; Hodge believed he could trace the killers, who had not been found.

framing.detail: The Omaha Daily Bee headed the brief 'White Devils' and called the attackers 'the murderers'.
